title: Three Marylebone Houses, a 56-Year Lease and a Promise to Pay
dek: In 1865 Octavia Hill took on three neglected houses bought with Ruskin's money, on the condition that they paid their way.

story.event: Taking on and managing three Marylebone houses for poor tenants on a paying basis
story.summary: In 1864 Octavia Hill persuaded John Ruskin to fund a housing scheme for poor families near her Marylebone home, on his condition that it pay a return; in early 1865 he bought the 56-year lease of three houses in Paradise Place for £750 and she took over their management. Collecting rents herself and setting aside a repair fund whose surplus the tenants spent, she reported in 1866 that the houses had paid five per cent and lost only £2 11s 3d to bad debts.
paragraphs: In April 1864, at 14 Nottingham Place in Marylebone, Octavia Hill wrote to a friend about a plan she had long carried: a house close by, put right for poor families she knew, small enough that she could know everyone in it. John Ruskin had promised the money by return of post. His own letter set the pace: he wanted to begin "very quietly and temperately, and to go on gradually."

He also set a condition. Hill later wrote that he showed her the scheme would be far more useful if it paid, since a working man ought to be able to pay for his own house. Her family recalled that he asked for five per cent, so that others might copy it, and that she protested, "Who will ever hear of what I do?" She agreed all the same. Agents balked once they heard who the house was for.

By April 1865 Ruskin had bought the remaining 56 years of the lease on three houses in a court close by, Paradise Place, for £750. Each still had a middleman landlord who could not be removed until midsummer, so repairs had to wait. "The plan promises to pay; but of this I say very little," she wrote; so much depended on management. She took her holiday early, she added, so she could manage with short ones later. When she took charge, the houses swarmed with vermin and the drains were blocked. She had them put right, but added no new fittings until tenants had shown they would care for them.

She collected the rents herself each week and insisted they be paid on time. A fixed sum went to repairs, and whatever was left at the quarter's end was spent on the house as each tenant in turn decided. In November 1866, after about a year and a half, she reported that the houses had paid five per cent on all the capital, repaid £48 of it, and lost just £2 11s 3d to bad debts.

Ruskin bought more property near by in 1866. By 1874, the Chartered Institute of Housing says, she ran fifteen schemes with about 3,000 tenants; in 1916 women who had worked with her founded the first professional body for housing workers.

quote.text: The perception of what is small is (the secret of) clear-sightedness; the guarding of what is soft and tender is (the secret of) strength.
quote.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics, tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #216
quote.connection: Hill's first report is built from small perceptions: blocked drains, the repair money left at a quarter's end, £2 11s 3d of bad debts. Laozi pairs that attention with guarding what is tender, as she tried to guard what she called the never-dying hope of her tenants.

reflection: Hill could have treated Ruskin's five per cent as a compromise of her ideals. Instead she let it keep her honest: if the houses paid, the method could spread beyond one generous friend. The figures she reported were small and exact, down to the shillings lost to bad debt.

She also planned her rest around the work, taking her holiday before the houses were handed over rather than hoping for one afterwards. If a demanding stretch is coming for you, it is reasonable to rest before it starts, not only once it is over, and to count the small numbers honestly as you go.
invitation: Before your next busy stretch begins, put one restful thing in the diary for this week, an early night or a free evening, and treat it as part of the preparation rather than a reward.

sources.title: Homes of the London Poor (1875), including "Cottage Property in London" (dated 1 November 1866)
sources.supports: Hill's own account: the plan long contemplated; Ruskin providing all the money and taking the risk, and showing her it should pay because a working man ought to be able to pay for his own house; three leasehold houses in her immediate neighbourhood; 56-year lease bought for £750; vermin, filthy papers hanging in strips, stopped drains and broken water supply; no new appliances until tenants proved capable; repair fund with the quarter's surplus spent as each tenant in turn decided; collecting rents herself and strict punctuality; work for tenants in slack seasons; persuading families to take two rooms; after about a year and a half, five per cent paid on all capital, £48 repaid, bad debts of £2 11s 3d; the 'never-dying hope' of the poor.

sources.title: Life of Octavia Hill as Told in Her Letters (ed. C. Edmund Maurice, 1913)
sources.supports: Letter of 19 April 1864 from 14 Nottingham Place on gathering poor friends in a house near by and Ruskin's promise by return of post; Ruskin's letter of 19 May 1864 ('very quietly and temperately, and to go on gradually'); family account of Ruskin asking for five per cent so others might follow, Hill's 'Who will ever hear of what I do?', and agents raising difficulties; letter of 11 December 1864 on legal delays; letter of 2 April 1865 on the purchase of 56 years of three houses, middleman landlords until midsummer, taking her holidays early, and 'The plan promises to pay; but of this I say very little'; three houses of six rooms each; Ruskin buying more houses by May 1866.

research_notes: Dates: some summaries (EBSCO) date the acquisition to 1864. Hill's letters show the plan agreed with Ruskin in April and May 1864, the purchase delayed by legal difficulties in December 1864, and the purchase completed by her letter of 2 April 1865; her essay of 1 November 1866 says the plan had been running about a year and a half. English Heritage, the Victorian Web and the CIH all give 1865, so the story dates the purchase to early 1865 and the plan to 1864. The return: Hill's 1866 essay says Ruskin wanted 'a fair percentage' and reports five per cent paid; the five per cent condition itself comes from the family account (by the editor's wife and her sisters, Hill's sisters) in the 1913 Life, and English Heritage says only 'a small profit'; the story attributes it to her family. Outcome figures (five per cent paid, £48 of capital repaid, £2 11s 3d of bad debts) are Hill's own report and have no independent check; they are attributed to her. Later expansion: the CIH says Ruskin bought 'five more' a year later; Hill's letter of 19 May 1866 says 'six more houses'; a letter printed with the date 15 April 1865 mentions freehold ground with five cottages and a large house, which seems misdated since the 2 April 1865 letter shows the first houses not yet in her control. The story says only that Ruskin bought more property near by in 1866. The 1874 figures (fifteen schemes, about 3,000 tenants) rest on the CIH alone and are attributed to it. English Heritage calls the houses 'almost new'; Hill called them well built but in a dreadful state of dirt and neglect; the story uses her description. The name Paradise Place comes from English Heritage and the Victorian Web; Hill's own essay says only 'in my own immediate neighborhood'. The slate listed the industry as construction; the episode is housing management, so the industry is given as housing (property management). Funding is mixed: private philanthropic capital from Ruskin, run on a commercial five per cent basis.
